title: Chaupai at nightfall
hook: the Benti Chaupai, now prayed as darkness comes

segments.voice: Yesterday, why worry, and your line, even the rock-creatures eat. Did you set one stone down? The nine shabads of Rehras are done. Now comes a prayer you already know, in a new light. Day four hundred fifteen.

Last thing at night, in a lot of houses, someone does the rounds. Back door locked. Stove knob checked, twice. A glance through the curtain at the street. A child's door pushed open an inch, just to hear the breathing. Nobody calls it a prayer. But it's one of the oldest things a household does: before the dark, make sure everyone is inside and kept. And the night still finds other ways in: a hospital ward, an empty flat, a long drive home. Today: Chaupai.
screen: `LAST THING AT NIGHT: THE ROUNDS.` → `EVERYONE INSIDE AND KEPT.` → `THE NIGHT STILL FINDS WAYS IN.`

segments.voice: After the nine shabads, Rehras moves from the Guru Granth Sahib to the Tenth Guru's words: the Benti Chaupai of Guru Gobind Singh, the same prayer many Sikhs said this morning. You spent ten days with it earlier on this path, so you know its first lines. In paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. May my mind stay at your feet. Take me as your own, and look after me. In the morning, those words go out with you into the day. In Rehras, they're said as the light is going, and they land differently. Shelter is what you ask for at dusk. Whoever does the rounds at night isn't looking for adventure. They want the door shut, a lamp on, someone keeping watch. That's the posture of the Chaupai in Rehras. And it isn't a frightened prayer. It was written by a Guru who faced real armies and real nights, and it never pretends danger isn't there. It simply asks, in the middle of it, to be kept. Right after it, Rehras carries the short savaiya and dohra you met at the close of that block: since I took hold of your feet, I look to no one else; leaving every other door, I've come to yours. So the order is a shape. Shelter me with your hand. I've stopped knocking on other doors. Yours is the one I'm at as night comes. Shelter for the night.
screen: `FROM THE NINE SHABADS TO THE TENTH GURU.` · `GIVE ME YOUR HAND AND KEEP ME.` · `AT DUSK, WHAT YOU ASK FOR IS SHELTER.` · `EVERY OTHER DOOR LEFT; YOURS AT NIGHT.` · then, large: `SHELTER FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read two lines at dusk. If you have the Chaupai on your phone or in a gutka, find the first two lines and read them slowly, aloud or under your breath: hamree karo haath dai rachhaa, pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa. If not, hold their meaning: protect me, giving me your hand; may the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Then picture the coming night: where you'll sleep, who's near, what you're carrying into it. Let the lines rest over it like a roof. The bell holds the time.
Chaupai, Guru Gobind Singh's Benti Chaupai, said in the morning and again inside Rehras as darkness comes: protect me, giving me your hand.
Your line: shelter for the night. Tonight, before you lock the door or turn out the light, say the first line of the Chaupai, or its meaning, once. Day four hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: In Rehras Sahib, after the nine shabads, Sikhs recite Guru Gobind Singh's Benti Chaupai, followed by a savaiya and a dohra; it is also one of the morning banis, and many Sikhs say it before a journey or at night.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rachhaa, protection; hamree karo haath dai rachhaa, protect me, giving me your hand.

trapdoor: what you thought: Chaupai at nightfall is a separate evening version of the prayer.
what it means: the same Benti Chaupai, said inside Rehras as dark comes, where its request becomes a plea for shelter for the night.

what a scholar hears: the Chaupai comes from the Dasam Granth; in the Rehat Maryada's Rehras it moves the prayer from Guru Granth Sahib shabads to the Tenth Guru's verse, then to the savaiya and dohra.
